citations.translation: freewomen who were standing in the heat of the day and were wailing and crying over me

notes.text: MD and others derive this word from Akkadian (i.e. nabû #2), but a connection with nbḥ seems equally possible. Cf. DJPA 725b end where nbḥ pael is to make various sounds. Etymologically nbḥ should appear without an Akkadian velar, hence nabû B could easily be the actual cognate to this root in Akkadian as well. In Akkadian, NBH does occur, but only in SB/NB texts. ( תיקו!) The form of the noun numbia (q.v.) matching the Akkadian noun in /u/ is probably the strongest evidence for the borrowing.

notes.text: The perfect is of this verb still appears regularly in Old Aramaic and Official Aramaic. In the later dialects it is regularly suppletively used in the pre-formative patterns for the even more irregular yhb. In Syriac (and less commonly CPA as a borrowing thereof) the dative preposition is assimilated to the end of the word, yielding the new root ntl, q.v.. In Babylonian, ntn and yhb merge producing ntb (see s.v. yhb). In all these instances, users should also consult s.v. yhb for possible semantic values.

notes.text: We have here separated between lqṭ "to glean, gather" and nqṭ "to seize", although the former meaning is found here in JBA as well. To judge by Hebrew and Arabic, though, the former is the original form of this root, meaning "to glean". Mandaic has only a third form LGṬ (see s.v. lqṭ), and is ubiquitous in the meaning "to seize", while in JBA (and in Syriac magic bowls) the form is almost always נקט. (In Geonic texts לקט must be viewed as a Hebraism.) At which stage the two forms split from a single root or should really be seen to be two different roots is unclear.

notes.text: The Greek of the Hosea passage seems to reflect a confused tradition since our MT text refers to וְלֵתֶךְ שְׂעֹרִים after already mentioning וְחֹמֶר שְׂעֹרִים. On the other hand, the interpretatin as a dry measure is an ancient guess and should be rejected.

citations.translation: and the dead one's name not be forgotten by his brethren

notes.text: Note that other than in Syriac, the Gt (DJPA incorrectly Dt!) is the more common usage for "to forget". The use of the af'el simply as "to forget" is well established in Mandaic, but the few apparent examples in targumic texts (e.g., at Deut 32:18) are almost certainly to be treated as Gt forms with assimilated taw, since the af'el is well-established in the meaning "to make forget" in those dialects. Syriac does have examples of Dt, rendered here "make oneself forget", but they are all in poetry and need to be seen as regular metris causa variants of Gt.

text.text: ואף מועדים נמי בעי לאתקוני להון

citations.translation: it is also even necessary to set up festivals

notes.text: Attested as a corruption in PTalm. see DJPA s.v. We disagree with DJBA 756n. s.v. (a suggestion which itself seems to conflict with what is stated there s.v. לם adv.) The suggestion to connect this word with the Syr. enclitic particle ܠܡ is perfectly reasonable, especially in light of the derivation of the latter from 'to say' as demonstrated by Kaufman in "An Assyro-Aramaic egirtu ša Šulmu." Pp. 119-27 of Essays on the Ancient Near East in Memory of Jacob Joel Finkelstein, M. de Jong Ellis, ed. (Hamden, Ct.: Archon, 1977). A literal English equivalent would thus be 'say' as a hypothetical particle. Alternatively, and perhaps preferably, connect with Ɂpm,Ɂm of Egyptian OfA, 'additionally, nonetheless' pronounced something like [ammĕ]. Note that נמי often occurs after such particles as אי nun would be due to redivision of syllables. It is unlikely that the form is connected with the unique Samaritan root of the same shape meaning "part".

notes.text: It is clear from the many Nabataean examples (among others), that the npš is the funeral monument bearing the memorial inscription. In the early KTMW text, however, it could be the funerary inscription or, less likely though most so think, the entombed spirit itself. Compare also np!yšh (not to be read nwyšh) in the Jauf inscription (Torrey, JAOS 54[1934]:29ff) in reference to a cemetery or memorial stone. In OT translations one may often translate npš + pron.suff. as "one's self", but the connotation is always more "one's existence". The earlier Syriac lexica seem to be unaware of the original meaning of this word as "throat, appetite", that is still to be found, at least as echoes, in the earliest Biblical and (possibly the poetic) texts.
